sources.title: Original synthetic teaching example. Numbers are assumptions, not company results.
sources.note: Original authored teaching note; values are assumptions.

claims.text: Contribution equals revenue less variable costs; fixed costs are outside this example.
Revenue rises from 100 to 150 while contribution falls from 40 to 30.

scenes.title: More revenue. Less left over.
scenes.narration: Can a business earn more revenue and have less left over? Yes. Watch what happens to the costs.
scenes.visualDescription: A single revenue bar contains variable costs and the remaining contribution. The baseline is $100 revenue, $60 variable costs and $40 contribution. These labels and colors persist throughout the explanation.

scenes.title: Start with what each sale leaves.
scenes.narration: Start with revenue. Subtract the variable costs of making those sales. What remains is contribution, before fixed costs.
scenes.visualDescription: The baseline revenue bar stays at $100. As the narration says subtract, a navy sweep identifies the $60 variable-cost portion; the remaining $40 then turns green as contribution. The animation illustrates decomposition of one baseline, not changing business results. Fixed costs are excluded.

scenes.title: Costs grew faster than revenue.
scenes.narration: Before, one hundred dollars of revenue minus sixty dollars of costs left forty. After, one hundred fifty minus one hundred twenty leaves thirty.
scenes.visualDescription: On a fixed dollar scale, the same bar changes from $100 revenue split into $60 costs and $40 contribution to $150 revenue split into $120 costs and $30 contribution. Costs grow faster, leaving a smaller contribution segment. A faint baseline remains for comparison. Intermediate values illustrate the transition only.

scenes.title: Growth needs an economics check.
scenes.narration: Revenue rose by fifty dollars. Contribution fell by ten. More sales alone do not tell you whether the economics improved.
scenes.visualDescription: The final bar remains at $150 revenue, $120 costs and $30 contribution. Relative to the retained $100/$60/$40 baseline, revenue is up $50, costs up $60 and contribution down $10. Fixed costs are excluded.

teaching.audience: Business students and anyone comparing growth with contribution economics.
teaching.goal: Predict contribution after revenue and variable costs change.
teaching.limit: Synthetic amounts cover the same period. Fixed costs, cash timing and real cost drivers are outside this example.

questions.question: Originally revenue was $100 and variable costs $60. With revenue $150 and variable costs $105, what is contribution? What cost level would keep the original contribution unchanged?
questions.answer: Contribution becomes $45, up $5. At $110 variable costs, contribution stays $40.
questions.explanation: $150 − $105 = $45 versus the original $40. Solve $150 − cost = $40 to get $110. These are contribution amounts before fixed costs, not profit.
